[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:bonzhik-khyungnak] Marpa Kagyu tradition figure listed in Treasury of Lives. (BDRC P11MS159)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:olkhawa-drolgom-choyung] Trained as a physician by his father as a young man, Wolkhawa became a monk and went on to be one of the important teachers of the early Kagyu. He also had personal links with the Sakya and Zhije. Wolkhawa specialized in teachings on how to develop compassion. (BDRC P5167)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:ga-lotsawa-zhonnu-pel] Ga Lotsāwa Zhonnu Pel was one of the most important figures in the transmission of Mahākāla practice in Tibet. He spent years in Bodhgaya and transmitted core Kagyu teachings such as the Six Yogas of Nāropa and the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra . He was a teacher to Lama Zhang , the First Karmapa , and Pakmodrupa Dorje Gyelpo . (BDRC P3674)
Andalusian author of Hayy ibn Yaqzan.

[rigpa-wiki:Karmapa Changchub Dorje] [rigpa-wiki:Karmapa] [rigpa-wiki:Düsum Khyenpa] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:karmapa-i] The First Karmapa, Dusum Khyenpa, was the founder of the Karma Kagyu tradition. A native of Kham, he was initially ordained and educated as a Kadam monk. After spending thirty years in U-Tsang studying with Gampopa and other disciples of Marpa and Milarepa , he returned to Kham where he remained for twenty years, establishing a number of monasteries, including Karma Gon . Then, at the age of seventy, he returned to Tibet, establishing Tsurpu Monastery in Tolung, the seat of the subsequent Karmapas. According to legend, when he was sixteen a group of ḍākinī gave him a hat made from the hair of 100,000 ḍākinī, which is visible only to the most advanced practitioners. He said to have predicted the conditions of his rebirth and instructed his disciples to find and trai…

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:phagmo-drupa] Pakmodrupa was a disciple of Gampopa and is one of the earliest patriarchs of the Kagyu tradition. His monastery, Densatil , which he founded in 1158, was the training ground for most of the founders of the Kagyu sub-traditions, such as Taklungtangpa and Jikten Gonpo , who went on to establish the Taklung and Drigung Kagyu, respectively. He integrated teachings that he received from Kadam, Sakya and, in vision, Zhije instructors into those he received from Gampopa. A widely learned but humble monk, he gave a clear priority to meditation over textual scholarship and philosophical reflection. His collected works have only recently been published in full. (BDRC P127)
[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:pakmodrupa-dorje-gyalpo] Texts by and about Pakmodrupa Dorje Gyalpo (1110–1170), a disciple of Gampopa and significant figure in early Kagyü history:
Founder of the Quanzhen school.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:khyungtsangpa-yeshe-lama] Khyungtsangpa is primarily remembered for his key role in the transmission of the Rechung Nyengyu. These teachings were not tied to any particular branch of the Kagyu, although it has been more often associated with the Drukpa Kagyu than with any other. (BDRC P5899)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gompa-tsultrim-nyingpo] Gompo Tsultrim Nyingpo, popularly known as Gomtsul, served as abbot of Daklha Gampo , the 'headquarters' of the Kagyu school, for nineteenth years following the death of his uncle Gampopa. He played an important historical role in his mediation of warring factions associated with different monastic lineages in the Lhasa area during the twelfth century. He was in charge of restoring the J okang Temple , since it had suffered serious damage during the fighting. He founded a monastery named Tsur Lhalung in Tolung. The most renowned among his disciples was Lama Zhang Yudrakpa . (BDRC P1845)
[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:gompa-tsultrim-nyingpo] Texts by and about Gompa Tsultrim Nyingpo (sgom pa tshul khrims snying po, 1116–1169), the eldest nephew of Gampopa:
[lineage-seed:kadam-lineage:khedrup-rinchen-drag] Later Kadampa master who consolidated lamrim and lojong lineages.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tropu-gyeltsa-rinchen-gon] Gyeltsa Rinchen Gon was a disciple of Pakmodrupa . He founded Tropu Monastery , which later became the seat of the Tropu Kagyu tradition initiated by his disciple, Tropu Lotsāwa Jampa Pel . Rinchen Gon was the uncle of Kunden Repa , although some sources have it that the two were brothers. (BDRC P1508)
57 m Liao-style brick pagoda from the Liao or early Jin dynasty.
Berber dynasty that replaced the Almoravids.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:katokpa-dampa-deshek] Katok Dampa Deshek Sherab Sengge was the founder, in 1159, of the first Nyingma monastery, Katok Dorjeden . The brother of Pakmodrupa Dorje Gyelpo , he studied under prominent lamas of the Nyingma, Kadam, Sakya, and Kagyu traditions, including the First Karmapa , Gampopa , and Sonam Tsemo . An expert in Nyingma tantra, his compositions are collected in nine volumes. (BDRC P1314)
[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:lama-zhang-tsondru-drakpa] Texts by and about Lama Zhang Tsöndrü Drakpa (bla ma zhang brtson 'grus grags pa, 1123–1193), founder of the Tsalpa Kagyü:
[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:nyang-ral-nyima-ozer] Texts composed or revealed by the important tertön Nyangral Nyima Özer (nyang ral nyi ma 'od zer, 1124–1192):
Commentator on Aristotle in al-Andalus.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:barompa] Barompa, one of the main disciples of Gampopa , initiated the Barom Kagyu lineage, one of the major Kagyu lineages. He founded Barom Monastery in Nakchu, in 1160, and several monasteries in Kham. Members of his lineage, although no longer very numerous, may be found today in Nangchen in Kham, in Nakchu as well as in Bodhanath, Nepal. (BDRC P1856)

[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-indian:shakyashribhadra] Texts by and about the Kashmiri master Śākyaśrībhadra (shā kya shrī bzang po, 1127–1225), who in 1204 travelled to Tibet, where he became the teacher of a number of important lamas, including Sakya Paṇḍita Kunga Gyaltsen:
[lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:shakyashri-bhadra] Kashmiri pandita; teacher of Sakya Pandita and many Sarma masters.
[lineage-seed:lamdre-lineage:shakyashri-bhadra-lamdre] Kashmiri pandita who taught Sakya Pandita and lamdré-adjacent scholastic lineages.

[rigpa-wiki:Lingje Repa Pema Dorje] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lingje-repa] Lingrepa Pema Dorje was a student of Pakmodrupa and the main teacher Tsangpa Gyare , who founded the Drukpa Kagyu tradition. He is frequently credited with founding a "Lingre Kagyu" school, though this is historically inaccurate. He initially developed the site that Tsangpa Gyare would build into Ralung Monastery . He is widely regarded as the one Tibetan who best exemplifies the Indian ideal of the Mahasiddha. (BDRC P910)

[rigpa-wiki:Tulku Pema Dorje] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lingrepa-pema-dorje] Lingrepa Pema Dorje was a student of Pakmodrupa and the main teacher Tsangpa Gyare , who founded the Drukpa Kagyu tradition. He is frequently credited with founding a "Lingre Kagyu" school, though this is historically inaccurate. He initially developed the site that Tsangpa Gyare would build into Ralung Monastery . He is widely regarded as the one Tibetan who best exemplifies the Indian ideal of the Mahasiddha. (BDRC P910)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chegompa-sherab-dorje] Chegompa Sherab Dorje is a mystifying figure for students of Tibetan Buddhism. He is widely accepted as a Kadampa, and certainly does hold a Kadam lineage. Still, in his best-known work he lays emphasis on simultaneous Mahāmudrā teachings, which were usually not in favor with Kadampas. Some think he had connections with the Tselpa Kagyu, although more certainly he was affiliated with the Tropu Kagyu. He was important for the transmission of the Kadam text known as the Example Teachings ( dpe chos ) and wrote a commentary on it, but he is probably best known for his Precious Heap of Instructions ( man ngag rin chen spungs pa ). Today his works are most greatly treasured by the Geluk. (BDRC P4892)

[rigpa-wiki:Lama Jangchub Rinpoche] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gomchung-sherab-jangchub] Gomchung Sherab Jangchub was a nephew of Gampopa and a younger brother of Gomtsul. He served as the third abbot of Daklha Gampo after the death of Gomtsul. (BDRC P1841)
Systematizer of Neo-Confucianism.

[rigpa-wiki:Yelpa Yeshe Tsek] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:yelpa-yeshe-tsek] Texts by and about the master Yelpa Yeshe Tsek (yel pa ye shes brtsegs, 1134–1194), a prominent disciple of Pakmodrupa Dorje Gyalpo (1110–1170) and founder of the Yelpa Kagyü:

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:dakpo-duldzin] Dakpo Duldzin was the fourth abbot of Daklha Gampo , the earliest Kagyu Monastery. He was a disciple of the monastery’s third abbot, Gomchung Sherab Jangchub , and was responsible for the construction of the main temple at the monastery, a building of forty columns. (BDRC P1850)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lhachug-kharwa-nyida-o] Lhachuk Kharwa was one of the four main disciples of Lama Zhang Yudrakpa . He founded the Lhachuk Monastery in 1193 and became the abbot of Tsel Monastery in 1210. During his abbacy, or soon after his death, the Tselpa Kagyu spread in the westernmost parts of the Tibetan Plateau. (BDRC P4139)

[rigpa-wiki:Chöjé Marpa Sherab Yeshé] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:marpa-sherab-yeshe] Marpa Sherab Yeshe was the founder of the Martsang Kagyu, one of a number of lineages that descended through disciples of Pakmodrupa . In 1167 he founded Sho Monastery , which was a major educational center in Kham, and the mother monastery of the Martsang Kagyu. (BDRC P1GS56176)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsangton-dorje-gyeltsen] Tsangton Dorje Gyeltsen, a close disciple of Katokpa Dampa Deshek , was the second abbot of Katok Monastery , from 1192 to his death in 1227. (BDRC P7894)
Ethiopian dynasty associated with the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela (c. 1200).
Wrote the Mishneh Torah and the Guide for the Perplexed.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rokam-nyima-sherab] Rokam Nyima Sherab served and studied with Zhang Yudrakpa before he founded his own monastery at Rokam . He was a significant figure in the early history of the Tselpa Kagyu. He initiated a lineage belonging to the Bar Tsel, the ‘Middle Lineage of the Tselpa Kagyu.’ (BDRC P2470)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drubtob-nyakre-sewo] Drubtob Nyakre Sewo was a disciple of Pakmodrupa and Jikten Gonpo . He founded Legon Chokyi Podrang in Drayab, and is is remembered for producing numerous miracles via means of urination. His songs of realization and autobiography has survived. (BDRC P1KG4203)
[lineage-seed:rinzai-lineage:eisai] First to establish Rinzai Zen formally in Japan after study in Song China.
Brought Rinzai Zen to Japan.
[lineage-seed:lamdre-lineage:sonam-tsemo] Second Sakya patriarch; systematized lamdré literature.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:taklungtangpa-tashi-pel] Taklungtangpa, one of the main disciples of Pakmodrupa , stands at the head of the Taklung Kagyu lineage. He founded Taklungtang Monastery in about the year 1180. (BDRC P2649)
Formation of the Iroquois League under the Great Law of Peace; the date is debated.
[lineage-seed:islam:chishti] Founder of the Chishti order in the Indian subcontinent.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jigten-sumgon] Jikten Gonpo is credited with the founding of Drigung Til Monastery in 1179 and the establishment of the Drigung Kagyu tradition. He was a close disciple of Pakmodrupa and briefly administered Densatil following Pakmodrupa's death. (BDRC P16)
Established the Chishti chain in South Asia.
[lineage-seed:shangpa-kagyu-lineage:kyergangpa] Third holder in the seven-precious Shangpa transmission line.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gyerton-tsultrim-sengge] Gyergom Tsultrim Sengge, a student of Pakmodrupa , was the founder of both the Shukseb Monastery , in 1181, and the Shukseb Kagyu lineage. Although primarily a follower of Kagyu teachings, he is also regarded as a lineage holder for the So Tradition of the Zhije. (BDRC P00AG02484)
[lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:dragpa-gyaltsen] Third Sakya patriarch.
[lineage-seed:lamdre-lineage:dragpa-gyaltsen] Third Sakya patriarch and lamdré lineage holder.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:nyamme-shakya-yeshe] Nyamme Śākya Yeshe is mainly significant for being the successor of Zhang Yudrakpa . Starting in around 1187, he served as the second abbot of Tsel Gungtang Monastery . (BDRC P8711)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:kunden-repa] An important disciple of Pakmodrupa , Kunden Repa figured in the origins of the Tropu lineage of the Kagyu. He was a nephew or younger brother of Gyeltsa Rinchen Gon , the founder of the tradition, and an uncle of Tropu Lotsāwa . (BDRC P1507)

Large white dagoba of Polonnaruwa, built by Queen Subhadra, consort of Parakramabahu I (12th century CE).

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gurawa-tsultrim-dorje] Gurawa Tsultrim Dorje was the successor of Jikten Gonpo as abbot of Drigung Monastery . Usually he is counted as the second abbot, although some sources name him the first. (BDRC P2210)
Founder of the Illuminationist school of Islamic philosophy, combined Neoplatonism with Islamic mysticism.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:ngok-kunga-dorje] Ngok Kunga Dorje was a prominent member of the Ngok family lineage of Hevajra practice. Although he never became a monk, he founded a monastery called Zhung Treuzhing . (BDRC P8729)
[rigpa-wiki:Drupchen Khepa Nyima Bum] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:nyima-bum] Texts by and about Nyima Bum (nyi ma 'bum, 1158–1213), alias Khepa Nyibum (mkhas pa nyi 'bum):
Founded the Jogye tradition of Seon.

[rigpa-wiki:Tsangpa Gyaré Yeshe Dorje] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:tsangpa-gyare-yeshe-dorje] Texts by and about Tsangpa Gyare Yeshe Dorje (gtsang pa rgya ras ye shes rdo rje, 1161–1211), the founder of Druk Monastery:

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chel-lotsawa-chokyi-zangpo] Chel Lotsāwa Chokyi Zangpo was a member of the Chel family, which controlled several monasteries in Tsang and was known for producing multiple translators. He traveled to India as a layperson and became a monk at Nālandā Monastery under  Śākyaśrībhadra , whom he met again in Tibet. He produced at least eleven translations that are preserved in the Tengyur. (BDRC P3939)

[rigpa-wiki:Tulku Dorje Dradül] [rigpa-wiki:Dorje Zangpo] [rigpa-wiki:Dorje Lingpa] [rigpa-wiki:Dorje Drakpa] [rigpa-wiki:Dorje Dechen Lingpa] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:dorje-khyung] Dorje Khyung was a disciple of Gurawa Tsultrim Dorje and Jikten Gonpo Rinchen Pel. (BDRC P1AG15)
[lineage-seed:soto-lineage:tiantong-rujing] Chinese Caodong master who transmitted the robe and bowl to Dogen in the Song period.
[lineage-seed:shangpa-kagyu-lineage:tishri-repa] Shangpa lineage holder listed in Treasury of Lives Shangpa Kagyu tradition.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:nyo-gyelwa-lhanangpa-sanggye-rinchen] One of the most important disciples of Jikten Gonpo , Nyo Gyelwa Lhanangpa Sanggye Rinchen founded a significant sub-branch of the Drigungpa, one that continued to be important in Bhutan until the seventeenth century under the name of the Lhapa. He had a reputation in his time as one of the most generous patrons of the monastic order. (BDRC P15)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tishri-repa-sherab-sengge] Tishrī Repa Sherab Sengge was perhaps the most important disciple of Barompa Dharma Wangchuk , although he was also closely associated with Lama Zhang and other early Kagyu patriarchs. In 1196 he went to stay in the Tangut kingdom where he remained in his capacity as court preceptor for thirty years. (BDRC P5133)
Andalusian Sufi master whose doctrine of the unity of being was highly influential.
[lineage-seed:zhije-chod-lineage:rokben-sherab-wo] Chöd and Zhije practitioner listed in Treasury of Lives.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rogben-sherab-o] Rok Bande Sherab Wo was a Nyingma scholar and yogi who was a major figure in the transmissions of the Guhyagarbha Tantra and the "later lineage" of Zhije tradition of Padampa Sanggye . (BDRC P4301)
[lineage-seed:zhije-chod-lineage:zarawa-kelden-yeshe-sengge] Zhije lineage holder in the Tingri tradition of Phadampa Sangye.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:spyan-snga-rin-chen-bzang-po] Chennga Rinchen Zangpo was a disciple of  Jikten Gonpo Rinchen Pel , the founder of  Drigung Til Monastery . He spent much of his life in Rebkong, spreading the Drigung teaching to lay disciples. (BDRC P11MS249)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:zarawa-kalden-yeshe-sengge] Zarawa Kelden Yeshe Sengge was one of the four foremost disciples of Pakmodrupa . Either Zarawa or perhaps his own disciple Chokyi Monlam might be considered the founder of the Yabzang Kagyu lineage. He was the founder, in 1158, of Zara Monastery . (BDRC P4329)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sanggye-dorje] Sanggye Dorje was the second abbot of Rokam Monastery . (BDRC P4168)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:yabzang-choje-chokyi-monlam] Yabzang Choje Chokyi Monlam was founder of the Yabzang Kagyu lineage, named after Yabzang Monastery , which he founded in 1206. (BDRC P4322)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:pomdrakpa] Pomdrakpa Sonam Dorje was an important early Karma Kagyu lineage holder; he was a student of Sanggye Rechen and a teacher of the Second Karmapa, Karma Pakshi, whom he identified as the reincarnation of the First Karmapa. He took over and renovated Tasho Pomdrak monastery. (BDRC P2438)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rinchen-sherab] Zhikpo Rinchen Sherab was the younger brother of Rokben Sherab O and a disciple of the same teacher, a man named Tenne. He studied at Drigung under that monastery's second abbot, Gurawa Tsultrim Dorje. (BDRC P4298)
Founded by Saladin.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tropu-lotsawa-jampa-pel] Among Tibetans of his day, Tropu Lotsāwa was most famous for building an eighty-cubit-high image of the future Buddha Maitreya, consecrated by Śākyaśrī in 1212. He was one of the significant figures in the early Tropu Kagyu, responsible for bringing the very important Indian Buddhist teachers Mitrayogin, Buddhaśrī, and Śākyaśrī to Tibet. Many of his translations, but only a few of his writings, are available today. (BDRC P4007)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chenga-chokyi-drag] Second Drikung Chungtsang.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chennga-drakpa-jungne] Chennga Drakpa Jungne served nearly two decades as Jikten Gonpo’s personal attendant. During the last half of his life he served first as abbot of Densatil , from 1208 to 1234, followed by twenty-one years as the fourth abbot of Drigung Monastery . (BDRC P132)
Qiyun Pagoda built by Jin dynasty in the 12th century in the grounds of the first Buddhist temple in China.
[lineage-seed:shangpa-kagyu-lineage:rigong-chokyi-sherab] Fourth holder of the uninterrupted Shangpa golden-doctrine line.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:wonre-darma-sengge] A nephew as well as disciple of Tsangpa Gyarepa , Darma Sengge   was the second abbot of Ralung Monastery . He is placed at the origin of the Bar Druk, or 'middle lineage' of the Drukpa school, and is the first of the line of Nine Lions who were so very important in the early history of the Drukpa Kagyu. (BDRC P912)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gar-dampa-chodingpa] Śākya Pel, or Gar Dampa Chodingpa, was a disciple of Jikten Gonpo . He wrote one of the three earliest works on the Gongchik , the Single Intention , and he was one of the three masters who ‘opened’ the region of Tsari for retreatants and pilgrims. He founded Choding Monastery and, in the last days of his life, a monastery called Rinchen Ling . His reincarnations are known as the Garchen Rinpoche . (BDRC P813)
Edo kingdom in present-day Nigeria known for its bronze plaques.
[lineage-seed:bodong-lineage:kodrakpa] Received Kalachakra from Vibhuticandra and propagated a distinct Bodong lamdré line.
Founder of the Franciscans.

[rigpa-wiki:Sakya Trizin Kunga Tashi] [rigpa-wiki:Sakya Pandita Kunga Gyaltsen] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:sakya-trichen] Texts by and about Kyabgön Sakya Gongma Rinpoche, Ngawang Kunga Tekchen Palbar (ngag dbang kun dga' theg chen dpal 'bar, b. 1945), the 41st Sakya Trizin:
[lineage-seed:lamdre-lineage:sakya-pandita] Fourth patriarch; authoritative lamdré commentator.
[lineage-seed:ra-luk-lineage:sakya-pandita-yamantaka] Systematized Yamantaka commentarial literature in the Sakya school.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:kodrakpa-sonam-gyeltsen] Kodrakpa Sonam Gyeltsen is best known as a teacher of the Six Limbed Yoga , the completion process practice of the Kālacakra Tantra . He did not belong to any one particular lineage, although it might be said that he belonged to this particular Kālacakra lineage together with a combination of general Kagyu with the Lamdre lineage of Zhama. (BDRC P1514)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:pajo-drukgom-zhigpo] Pajo Drukgom Zhikpo is a figure of particular importance to Bhutanese history. A layperson, a Drukpa and a disciple of the second abbot of Ralung, he was regarded as a holder of three lineages: Dzogchen, Mahāmudrā of the Drukpa Kagyu, and Zhije. Prophecies guided him to his later career in Bhutan, where he gained considerable political influence. His Drukpa school came into clashes with the Lhapa school, ultimately emerging victorious. This is the reason Bhutan came to be known as “Drukpa Country.” Pajo Drukgom Zhikpo established the first Drukpa monasteries in Bhutan. (BDRC P7852)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lorepa-wangchuk-tsondru] Lorepa is considered the founder of a branch of the Drukpa Kagyu called the Me Druk, or "Lower Druk." A very important teacher during his times, he exemplifies the life of solitary meditation under often difficult circumstances. He founded Tharpaling in Bhutan. (BDRC P4252)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:won-sherab-jungne] Won Sherab Jungne was the compiler and author of the core texts of the Single Intention . A philosophical cycle that revolves around key statements made by Jigten Gonpo , it is still regarded as a one of the main teachings of the Drigung Kagyu lineage. It is for this and for his important biography of his teacher that he is best known today. (BDRC P131)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:won-sonam-drakpa] Won Sonan Drakpa, a great-nephew of Jigten Gonpo , was the third abbot of Drigung Monastery . He held the chair from 1222 until his death 1234. (BDRC P4587)
[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:gotsangpa-gonpo-dorje] Texts by and about Götsangpa Gönpo Dorje (rgod tshang pa mgon po rdo rje, 1189–1258):
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:samlingpa] Samlingpa, about whom little is known, founded the Kagyu monastery Samling in the Lower Nyang Valley, Tibet. (BDRC P4206)
Largest dagoba of Polonnaruwa, built by King Nissanka Malla (1187-1196 CE) modelled on Ruwanwelisaya.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:kuyalwa-rinchen-gon] Kuyelwa Rinchen Gon was the second abbot of Taklung Monastery , a post he assumed in 1210. The monastery buildings were expanded during his abbacy and the number of the monks increased tremendously. (BDRC P1784)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:zhonnu-rinchen] Zhonnu Rinchen was the third abbot of Rokam Monastery . (BDRC P1AG7)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jangsem-choje-sonam-gyeltsen] Jangsem Choje Sonam Gyeltsen was a thirteenth-century practitioner of the Aural Lineage of Rechungpa. He was the father of Kunden Rema . (BDRC P5895)
Oldest tahoto in Japan, built 1194.

[rigpa-wiki:Guru Tsewang] [rigpa-wiki:Guru Tashi] [rigpa-wiki:Guru Jotsé] [rigpa-wiki:Guru Jober] [rigpa-wiki:Guru Chökyi Wangchuk] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:guru-tashi] Texts by and about the famous Nyingma historian Guru Tashi (gu ru bkra shis, b. 18th C.) of Takmo Gang:

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:guru-jober] Guru Jober was the grandson of Gyelwa Zhangton and the nephew of Nyima Bum, from whom he received the Nyingtik transmission. His chief disciple was Trulzhik Sengge Gyabpa. (BDRC P631)
Founder of the Shadhili order.
Five-sided stupa built by King Narapatisithu in 1196.
[lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:chag-lotsawa] Translator who brought Kalachakra to Tibet from Kashmir.
[rigpa-wiki:Chak Lotsawa Chöjé Pal] [lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:chak-lotsawa] Sakya translator active in the thirteenth-century imperial court.
[lineage-seed:ra-luk-lineage:chag-lotsawa-yamantaka] Sakya translator who also transmitted Yamantaka-related cycles.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:ras-pa-dkar-po] Repa Karpo was the principal disciple of Tishri Repa Sherab Sengge . The Mongolian Prince Godan appointed him religious leader of Nangchen, alongside Trewo Alu , who was appointed secular ruler. (BDRC P5137)
Zen Buddhism develops in Japan, emphasizing meditation and enlightenment
[lineage-seed:soto-lineage:dogen] Founder of Japanese Soto Zen after receiving transmission from Tiantong Rujing.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:zhonnu-sengge] Zhonnu Sengge is counted as the second of the “Nine Incomparable Lions,” patriarchs of the Drukpa Kagyu tradition. He was born into a prominent Drukpa family – his paternal uncle was Darma Sengge Sanggye Won , the first of the Nine Incomparable Lions and the student of Tsangpa Gyare , who founded the Drukap tradition. He served as the third abbot of Ralung Monastery . (BDRC P913)
Primordial or cosmic Adam in Lurianic and earlier kabbalistic cosmology; linked to Metatron-Enoch exaltation themes.
Saman is a local or syncretic deity absorbed into Southeast Asian Buddhist Buddhist cult, linked to mountains, rain, protection.
Antlered spectral hunter of Windsor Forest; often treated as a later folkloric reflex of horned lord motifs.
Inca creator god who emerged from Lake Titicaca, made the sun, moon, and stars, and taught civilization before departing across the sea.
Sky Father in Māori cosmogony; locked in primal embrace with Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) until separated by their children.
Earth Mother in Māori cosmogony; with Ranginui forms the primordial parental pair whose separation enables the world of light and life.
Baltic thunder god, one of the clearest likely reflexes of the Indo-European thunderer complex.
Baltic divine horse twins, close parallels to Vedic Ashvins and Greek Dioscuri.
Baltic chthonic deity of cattle and the dead; rival of Perkūnas. Cognate with Slavic Veles and reconstructed PIE Welnos.
Baltic sun goddess who weaves fate and drives a solar chariot. Major figure in Baltic religion.
Baltic fate goddess who determines human destiny at birth; sometimes manifested as a cuckoo.
Baltic sky god; the name is a clear reflex of PIE Dyēus and is the general word for god in Lithuanian/Latvian.
Baltic moon god; spouse of Saulė in Lithuanian folklore; associated with the calendar and fate.
Primordial cow in Norse cosmogony who licks Búri into being and nourishes Ymir with her milk.
Founded Sōtō Zen in Japan; Shōbōgenzō.
Naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads from Ile-Ife.
Large stupa modelled on Boudhanath, built by Lama Pradhar in the 13th century on a lake-side site in the Tawang region. Position approximate.
Hilltop chedi in Phrae, which tradition ascribes to the 13th century; contains a Buddha relic.
Mekong stupa reputedly enshrining the Buddha's breastbone, tradition dates to the 3rd century BCE (Ashoka), but the earliest structure is 8th-12th century; collapsed in 1975 and rebuilt.
Stupa in Sinhalese style built c. 1200 by monk Sapada. Position approximate.
Principal temple of Nakhon Si Thammarat, founded perhaps in the 8th century; its Sinhalese-style Phra Borommathat Chedi (37 m), a major relic stupa, is attributed to about the 13th century.
[lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:galo-namgyel-dorje] Sakya siddha associated with Vajrayogini and protector cycles.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drakpa-tsondru] Drakpa Tsondru, was the fifth abbot of Densatil Monastery from 1235 to 1267. He was a disciple and nephew of Drakpa Jungne, his predecessor at Densatil, and is counted as one of "Eight Mountain Dwellers," a group of Drigung monks who resided in Tsari and were disciples of both Drakpa Jungne and Won Sherab Jungne. Together with Jikten Gonpo and Drakpa Jungne he is named one of "Three Emperors of Drigung." (BDRC P1AG9)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sanggye-yarjon] Sanggye Yarjon Sherab Lama was the third abbot of Taklung Monastery. He continued to expand the monastery, installing countless gold and silver images. Close to the Sakya, he met with Chogyel Pakpa at the age of seventy. (BDRC P1818)
Crusaders and Venetians take the Byzantine capital.
Largest contiguous land empire in history, connecting East and West.
Largest contiguous land empire in history, connecting East and West
Five Muslim dynasties ruling from Delhi.
[lineage-seed:islam:rumi] Persian poet and Sufi master of the Mevlevi tradition after Shams-i Tabrizi.
Persian poet; the Mevlevi order grew from his followers at Konya.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jamyang-gonpo] A disciple of Lorepa , Jamyang Gonpo was the main transmitter of the Lower Drukpa school. He was also an important teacher of the Chod tradition. (BDRC P4253)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chung-dorje-drakpa] Chung Dorje Drakpa was the fifth abbot of Drigung Monastery , a position he held from 1255 to 1278. (BDRC P2221)
[lineage-seed:shangpa-kagyu-lineage:sangye-tonpa] Fifth holder who began branching the Shangpa line to multiple disciples.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:yanggonpa-gyeltsen-pel] Yanggonpa Gyeltsen Pel is perhaps best known for his writings on retreat practice, Mahāmudrā exegesis, and commentary on the subtle body. He spent most of his life in Gungtang, and received teachings from Kodrakpa , Gotsangpa , Sakya Paṇḍita , and Chennga Drakpa Jungne , among other masters. Although primarily remembered as a Drukpa Kagyu master, his writings had wide influence on numerous Tibetan religious traditions. (BDRC P5262)

[rigpa-wiki:Gyalwa Phakpa Lha] [rigpa-wiki:Gyalwa Chokyang] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:gyalwa-yangonpa] Texts by and about the famous Drukpa Kagyü adept Yangönpa Gyaltsen Pal (yang dgon pa rgyal mtshan dpal, 1213–1258):
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sonam-pel] Nyemdowa Sonam Pel, the son of Nyemdowa Mawai Sengge, was a disciple of Drakpa Jungne, the fourth abbot of Drigung Monastery. (BDRC P3766)
Snorri Sturluson's handbook of skaldic poetry and myth.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jonub-yeshe-dorje] Jonub Dorje Yeshe was the eighth abbot of Drigung Monastery. A rare early abbot who was not from the Kyura clan that controlled Drigung, he is listed in some sources as a regent for the subsequent abbot, Chunyipa Dorje Rinchen, who was a child at the time of Yeshe Dorje's ascension. During his tenure Drigung revolted against Sakya-Mongol rule of Tibet and was thoroughly defeated; Drigung Monastery was destroyed, and Dorje Yeshe was forced to flee to Kongpo, where he remained until his death. (BDRC P8572)
Integrated Neoplatonic concepts into his Christian theology, particularly through Pseudo-Dionysius, exploring divine emanation.

[rigpa-wiki:Garwang Chökyi Gyaltsen] [rigpa-wiki:Chomden Rigpé Raldri] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:chomden-rigpe-raldri] Texts by and about Chomden Rigpé Raldri (bcom ldan rig pa'i ral gri, 1227–1305), a celebrated scholar connected with Narthang Monastery:
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tokkhawa-rinchen-sengge] Tokkhawa Rinchen Sengge was the sixth abbot of Drigung Til Monastery , serving from 1278 to 1284. (BDRC P2222)

[rigpa-wiki:Orgyenpa Rinchen Pal] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:orgyenpa-rinchen-pel] Orgyenpa Rinchen Pel is credited with originating the tradition of teaching known as the Orgyen Nyendrub, often listed as the last of the “Eight Great Chariots of the Practice Lineages.” He studied with the Drukpa Kagyu lama Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje and made two pilgrimages to India, first to Oḍḍiyāna and then to Vajrasana, where he received additional teachings and is said to have gained miraculous healing powers. (BDRC P1448)
West African empire famous for Mansa Musa and Timbuktu's learning centers.
West African empire famous for Mansa Musa and Timbuktu's learning centers
[lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:phagpa] Fifth patriarch; imperial preceptor.

[rigpa-wiki:Chögyal Pakpa] [rigpa-wiki:Chögyal Ngakgi Wangpo] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:chogyal-pakpa-lodro-gyaltsen] Texts by and about the great Sakya master Chögyal Pakpa Lodrö Gyaltsen (chos rgyal ’phags pa blo gros rgyal mtshan, 1235–1280):
[lineage-seed:hinduism:madhva] Founder of Dvaita Vedanta in the Udupi guru parampara.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sengge-sherab] Sengge Sherab was the fourth of the “Nine Incomparable Lions,” patriarchs of the Drukpa Kagyu tradition. Although never a throne holder of Ralung , he studied under the fourth abbot and trained the fifth. His main seat was the monastery Bardrok Dorje Ling . (BDRC P916)
[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsamchepa-drakpa-sonam] Chennga Tsamchepa Drakpa Sonam was the seventh abbot of Drigung Monastery , from 1284 to 1286. (BDRC P2223)
Chishti master in Delhi.
First major Thai kingdom.
Spanish Kabbalist associated with circulating the Zohar.
Wahdat al-wujud as part of the apophatic/nondual turn.
[lineage-seed:bon-lineage:druje-yungdrung] Revitalized Bön at Yeru Wensakha monastery.
[rigpa-wiki:Kunpang Doringpa] [lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:kunpang-thukje-tsondru] Transmitted Kalachakra and zhentong to Dolpopa.
[rigpa-wiki:Melong Dorje] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:melong-dorje] Texts by and about the great Dzogchen adept and lineage-holder Melong Dorje (me long rdo rje, 1243–1303):

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jangsem-gyelwa-yeshe] Jangsem Gyelwa Yeshe was the second abbot of Jonang Monastery . He first studied and practiced the teachings of the Karma Kagyu tradition. Then he traveled widely, meeting many other teachers, and especially studied extensively at Sakya monastery. He finally became the main disciple of Kunpang Tukje Tsondru at Jonang. (BDRC P1511)
Monolithic statues carved on Easter Island.
Slave-soldier dynasty that defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sanggye-on-drakpa-pel] Sanggye Wonpo Drakpa Pel was the founder of Riwoche Monastery , in 1276, and served as its first abbot, until 1296. A disciple of Sanggye Yarjon , he was briefly abbot of Taklung , from 1272 to 1273, until he was forced out by his cousin Tashi Lama. He is said to have been a reincarnation of Gampopa . (BDRC P1019)
Hulagu Khan ends the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad.
Christian mystic who synthesized Neoplatonic ideas, emphasizing the soul's direct union with God and the process of spiritual ascent.
14-metre pagoda tower in the Tran dynasty homeland, 1262; built to commemorate Tran kings; of stupa-pagoda type. Position approximate.
src: Phổ Minh Pagoda, Nam Định: Vietnamese national special relic (Tran dynasty, 1262)

items.d: [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:kumaradza] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:kumaradza] Kumāradza was a holder of the Dzogchen Nyingtik lineage. He was a disciple of Melong Dorje and the master of Longchenpa. (BDRC P2349)
[lineage-seed:soto-lineage:keizan] Great systematizer who spread Soto practice widely through provincial temples in Japan.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:bsod-nam-dpal-dren] Sonam Peldren was a nomadic woman remembered for miraculous actions and pronouncements, an unusual death, and for claiming to be an emanation of the deity Dorje Pakmo, despite never having received religious teachings in her lifetime. Ganden Khacho Ling nunnery, currently affiliated with the Geluk tradition, is built upon the reputed site of her death in the village of Ya Nga Chamda in Driru. (BDRC P10MS14674)
Manuscript of the Poetic Edda, chief source for Norse myth.
Mongol-ruled China, established by Kublai Khan.
Mongol-ruled China, established by Kublai Khan
[lineage-seed:inchagiri-sampradaya:nivruttinath] Nath yogi who initiated his younger brother Dnyaneshwar into the Nath sect after receiving initiation from Gahininath.
Cosmos and afterlife column.
[lineage-seed:rinzai-lineage:muso-soseki] Influential Rinzai master, landscape designer, and teacher to court and samurai circles.
[lineage-seed:inchagiri-sampradaya:dnyaneshwar] Maharashtrian sant and Nath tradition poet-saint. Author of Dnyaneshwari; remembered in Inchagiri memory as Kad-Siddheshwar Maharaj.
[rigpa-wiki:Pang Mipham Gönpo] [lineage-seed:bodong-lineage:pang-lotsawa] Bodong translator and lineage holder listed in Treasury of Lives.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:dorje-rinchen] Chunyipa Dorje Rinchen was the ninth abbot of Drigung Monastery, from 1287 to 1314. He supervised the rebuilding of the monastery following its destruction by the Sakya-Mongol armies in 1290. (BDRC P2225)
Tibetan-style stupa designed by Nepalese architect Araniko, built 1271-1279 for Kublai Khan, one of the oldest surviving Yuan structures in Beijing. Position approximate.
Kabbalistic text circulated in Spain by Moses de León.
Kabbalah's Ein Sof + Sefirot + Shekhinah.
[lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:kunpang-chodrak-pelzang] Predecessor at Jonang Monastery before Dolpopa's tenure.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:dorje-gyelpo] Nyergyepa Dorje Gyelpo was the tenth abbot of Drigung Monastery , from 1314 to 1350. Tradition holds that he was a reincarnation of Padmasambhava. (BDRC P2226)

[rigpa-wiki:Rangjung Dorje] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:karmapa-iii] The Third Karmapa, Rangjung Dorje, was a prominent Karma Kagyu hierarch who also held Nyingma and Chod lineages. He was likely the first man to carry the title of Karmapa, following his identification by Orgyenpa Rinchen Pel as the reincarnation of Karma Pakshi , whom Orgyenpa posthumously identified as the reincarnation of Dusum Khyenpa . He spent much of his life traveling across Tibet and made two visits to the Yuan court in China. (BDRC P66)
[lineage-seed:zhije-chod-lineage:rangjung-dorje-chod] Third Karmapa who received and propagated Zhije and Chöd transmissions.
[rigpa-wiki:Yungtön Dorje Pal] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:yungton-dorje-pal] Texts by and about Yungtön Dorje Pal (g.yung ston rdo rje dpal, 1284–1365):
[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:third-karmapa-rangjung-dorje] Texts by and about the Third Karmapa, Rangjung Dorje (karma pa rang byung rdo rje, 1284–1339):
Late-Bagan stupa completed in 1284 by Narathihapate, the last major monument before the Mongol sack.
[lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:nyawon-kunga-pel] Fourteenth-century Jonang master of Kalachakra exegesis.
Temple with a Sinhalese-style bell-shaped chedi supported by 39 elephants, probably built by Ramkhamhaeng. Position approximate.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drigung-lotsawa-manikashrijnana] Drigung Lotsāwa Maṇikaśrījñāna, who was one of Dolpopa ’s fourteen major disciples, was a master of Sanskrit studies. He also held the monastic seat of the great Kagyu monastery of Drigung as a young man. After studying with Dolpopa, Drigung Lotsāwa became an ardent defender of the zhentong view and spread the Kālacakra teachings of the Jonang tradition. Toward the end of his life he taught the Vimalaprabhā for eight years at Jonang Monastery . (BDRC P2252)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sengge-gyelpo] Sengge Gyelpo, the son of Sengge Rinchen , was the seventh abbot of Ralung Monastery and the sixth of the “Nine Incomparable Lions,” patriarchs of the Drukpa Kagyu tradition. He was responsible for building a main temple at the monastery. (BDRC P606)
[rigpa-wiki:Butön Rinchen Drup] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:buton] Texts by and about the great Sakya lama Butön Rinchen Drup (bu ston rin chen grub, 1290–1364) of Shalu Monastery:
[lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:buton-rinchen-drup] Zhalu master who edited the Kangyur and taught across Sakya circles.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:buton-rinchen-drub] Buton Rinchen Drub, a Sakya lama raised in a Nyingma family, was the eleventh abbot of Zhalu Monastery , from 1320 to 1356. Some enumerations list him as the first abbot, as he significantly expanded the institution. He was an important teacher of the Prajñāpāramitā, and a key lineage holder of the Guhyasamāja and Kālacakra tantras as transmitted in the Geluk tradition, and the Kālacakra, Hevajra and Sampuṭa tantras as transmitted in the Sakya tradition. He is generally credited as the creator of the Tibetan Buddhist canon, the Kangyur and Tengyur, and his History of Buddhism is still widely read. In addition to his Sakya training he also studied in the Kadam and Kagyu traditions. (BDRC P155)

[lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:dolpopa-sherab-gyaltsen] Texts by and about Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen (dol po pa shes rab rgyal mtshan, 1292–1361), who was one of the most influential masters in Tibetan history. He trained in the Sakya tradition and then moved to Jonang Monastery, where he established a formidable yet controversial scholarly tradition.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:shangton-gyawo-sonam-drakpa] Zhangton Gyawo, who was one of Dolpopa ’s fourteen major disciples, studied widely in different traditions as a young man. Then he spent almost thirty years with Dolpopa, receiving all the great master’s teachings. For the last fifteen years of his life Zhangton taught the massive Vimalaprabhā commentary on the Kālacakra Tantra every year. (BDRC P2253)
Central temple of the Sukhothai Kingdom, with a lotus-bud chedi, founded under King Ramkhamhaeng (c. 1292). Position approximate.
Hindu-Buddhist empire in Java.
[lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:sabzang-mati-panchen] Jonang scholar and disciple in Dolpopa's circle.
[lineage-seed:zhije-chod-lineage:sabzang-mati-panchen-chod] Jonang master who also held Zhije and Chöd lineages.
Defender of contemplative prayer in Eastern Orthodoxy.
Advaita scholar and head of the Śṛṅgeri math; associated with the founding of Vijayanagara.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:rinchen-tsultrim] Rinchen Tsultrim, who was one of Dolpopa ’s fourteen major disciples, studied in many places as a young man, such as the Kagyu monastery of Tsurpu in U and Sakya Monastery in Tsang. From Dolpopa and his other major disciples, Rinchen Tsultrim received a vast number of teachings, especially from the Kālacakra tradition. He later lived and taught in central Tibet, emphasizing the study and practice of the Kālacakra. (BDRC P2256)

[rigpa-wiki:Gyalsé Tokmé Zangpo] [rigpa-wiki:Gyalsé Shenpen Tayé] [rigpa-wiki:Gyalsé Rinchen Namgyal] [rigpa-wiki:Gyalsé Lharjé] [rigpa-wiki:Gyalsé Lekden] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:gyalse-thogme-zangpo] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jamyang-konchok-zangpo] Jamyang Konchok Zangpo was the main disciple of the great adept Kunga Lodro . He was the fourteenth holder of the monastic seat of Jonang Monastery and also held the same position at several other monasteries during his lifetime. He was a master of many traditions, but especially of the Jonang teachings of the Kālacakra and the Sakya teachings of Lamdre. (BDRC P2464)
Oldest temple in Chiang Mai, founded by King Mangrai in 1297; Chang Lom elephant chedi.
Long-lasting empire that bridged Europe, Asia, and Africa.
Long-lasting empire that bridged Europe, Asia, and Africa
[lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:yakde-panchen] Jonang scholar active in the fourteenth-century scholastic revival.
[lineage-seed:bodong-lineage:yakde-panchen-bodong] Scholar associated with both Jonang and Bodong Kalachakra circles.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:yakde-panchen-tsondru-dargye] Yakde Paṇchen Tsondru Dargye, a Sakyapa scholar, was the founder of Evam Monastery . He is said to have studied under hundred and eight teachers, including many of the great figures of his era such as the Third Karmapa , the First Zhamarpa , Buton Rinchen Drub , Dolpopa , Longchenpa , and Tsongkhapa . (BDRC P4312)
Aztec earth-mother goddess who births the moon and stars; central to Mexica cosmogony involving sacrifice and celestial birth.
Orthodox monasteries on rock pillars in Thessaly.
The only stupa remaining in East Java, a Majapahit-period stone stupa near a spring in the Singosari region. Position approximate.
Temple with seven rows of 33 chedis of mixed styles at Si Satchanalai, 13th-14th century. Position approximate.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:puntsok-pelsang] Puntsok Pelzang, who was one of Dolpopa ’s fourteen major disciples, first studied extensively in the Kagyu tradition. After seeing a copy of Dolpopa’s Ocean of Definitive Meaning , he went to meet the great master and received many special teachings. He later lived and taught in U, initially at Sangpu Monastery and then at Kalapa Hermitage , which he founded. He mostly practiced and taught the Kālacakra tradition and the six-branch yoga. (BDRC P2413)
[rigpa-wiki:Jikdral Chokle Namgyal] [lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:chokle-namgyal] Disciple who continued the Jonang seat.

[rigpa-wiki:Sogan Rinpoche Natsok Rangdrol] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:longchen-rabjam] Texts by and about Longchenpa, or Longchen Rabjam (klong chen rab 'byams, 1308–1364), also known as Drimé Özer (dri med 'od zer), who is widely acknowledged as the greatest exponent of Dzogpachenpo, or the Great Perfection, in Tibetan history:

[rigpa-wiki:Longchenpa] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:longchenpa-drime-wozer] Longchenpa is considered one of the greatest philosophers and authors of the Nyingma tradition of Tibetan Buddhism. In his many writings he brought together disparate strands of Dzogchen teachings, both those based on Indian scriptures and on revelations. He trained in both Kadam and Sakya monasteries before receiving the Dzogchen Nyingtik transmissions from his teacher Kumāradza and in visions. Briefly banished from Tibet, he fathered children and established teaching lineages in Bhutan. (BDRC P1583)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:barawa-gyeltsen-pelzang] Je Barawa Gyeltsen Pelzang was the founder of the Barawa Kagyu, a branch of the Drukpa Kagyu which emerged in the fourteenth century and spread across Tibet and the Himalayan borderlands, including Bhutan and Sikkim. Je Barawa was a venerated teacher and religious leader with political influence in Bhutan. His major work, an exegesis on Buddhism, is entitled A Boat by which One Enters Liberation . (BDRC P1932)

[rigpa-wiki:Sönam Tsemo] [rigpa-wiki:Sonam Gyatso] [rigpa-wiki:Sönam Detsen] [rigpa-wiki:Lama Sonam Thayé] [rigpa-wiki:Lama Dampa Sönam Gyaltsen] [rigpa-wiki:Godrakpa Sönam Gyaltsen] [lineage-seed:sakya-lineage:sonam-gyaltsen] Sakya ruler and author of Clear Mirror of Royal Genealogy.
Stupa on the Sagaing hills, founded in 1312 by Ponya Shin. Position approximate.
[lineage-seed:islam:naqshband] Eponymous master of the Naqshbandi silsila, emphasizing silent dhikr.
Baha-ud-Din Naqshband and the order that bears his name.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:gharungwa-lhai-gyeltsen] Gharungwa Lhai Gyeltsen, who was one of Dolpopa ’s fourteen major disciples, studied at many Sakya and Kagyu monasteries before first meeting Dolpopa. After receiving the six-branch yoga and other instructions from Dolpopa, Gharungwa gained exceptional experience in meditation. He also received many profound transmissions from other major disciples of Dolpopa. Gharungwa became a great teacher and composed a number of important works, especially a biography of Dolpopa. (BDRC P2414)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:taklung-lotsawa-sakya-zangpo] Taklung Lotsāwa Śākya Zangpo was a fourteenth-century Taklung Kagyu monk. He was a student of many of the most prominent translators of his day, including Pang Lotsāwa and Jangchub Tsemo . He was known by the title of translator, but no translations credited to him survive. (BDRC P1333)
Elaborated hells and heavens; demonic hierarchies.
The Malian emperor's hajj, with its lavish gold, spread his fame across the Mediterranean world.
Main temple of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc.
Mexica settle on an island in Lake Texcoco.
Christian apophatic strand, with Cusa's coincidence of opposites.
Octagonal brick chedi 88 ft tall built by King Saen Phu in 1331. Position approximate.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:kunga-bum] Katokpa Kunga Bum was the eighth abbot of Katok Monastery , from 1357 to 1369. In his youth he travelled broadly in U-Tsang and Kham provinces and studied under a number of distinguished lamas of various Tibetan Buddhist Traditions of the time. Besides maintaining its tradition intact he introduced the Chod to Katok and composed a popular text on the practice. (BDRC P7964)
Author of the Muqaddimah, a pioneer of social theory.

[rigpa-wiki:Chökyi Drakpa] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chokyi-gyelpo] Chokyi Gyelpo was the eleventh abbot of Drigung Til Monastery . During his tenure, from 1350 to 1395, Drigung suffered a disastrous defeat by the Pakmodru ruler of Tibet, Jangchub Gyeltsen , and lost much of its influence. (BDRC P1485)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsongkhapa-lobzang-drakpa] Tsongkhapa Lobzang Drakpa was one of the most influential Tibetan Buddhist scholars of the last millennium. Born in Amdo, he traveled to U-Tsang in his youth, never to return to his homeland. He studied with numerous teachers of all traditions and engaged in many retreats resulting in his development of a fresh interpretation of Nāgārjuna's Madhyamaka view and a reinvigoration of the monastic Vinaya. Widely regarded as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, Tsongkhapa composed eighteen volumes of works of which the majority dealt with tantric subjects. He was the founder of Ganden Monastery, which became the central monastery of the Geluk tradition that was based on his teachings and writings. (BDRC P64)

He took teachings from masters in all traditions of his day, and, during the more than forty years of his abbacy of Taklung, oversaw an expansion of the monastery and its relations with other institutions. He was granted the title Guoshi from the Yongle Emperor of China the last year of his life. (BDRC P8425)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:drungchen-khachopa-namkha-gyeltsen] A prince of a ruling family of Markham, Drungchen Khachopa Namkha Gyeltsen studied with lamas of all the major traditions, founding a monastery in the Dzachu River Valley north of Chamdo called Namgyel Gang. [rigpa-wiki:Vanaratna] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:vanaratna] Vanaratna was a Bengali Tantric Buddhist master known in Tibet as "the last Indian paṇḍita." He traveled in Tibet three times in the first half of the thirteenth century. A master of the Kālacakra, he was a preceptor to some of the last heads of Pakmodru family, and enjoyed patronage from the members of the Rinpung family in Shigatse. Among his disciples were Rongton Sheja Kunrik , Go Lotsawa Zhonnu Pel , and Trimkhang Lotsāwa Sonam Gyatso ; the second of these students composed a biography, which was completed by the third. He was a Sanskrit scholar and served as translator to an Indian scholar Paṇḍit Vanaratna for five years. Nicholas of Cusa is known for his philosophy of learned ignorance (docta ignorantia) and his exploration of the infinite nature of God. He proposed that God is both immanent and transcendent, and that the universe is in a constant process of unfolding. His ideas about the coincidence of opposites and the dynamic relationship between God and creation are closely aligned with later Panentheistic and process thought.

[rigpa-wiki:Tsangnyön Heruka] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tsangnyon-heruka] Perhaps best known today as the author and publisher of the famous biography and collected songs of Milarepa, Tsangnyon Heruka was also one of the most influential mad yogins of Tibet. He is famous for having renovated the Svayambhū Stūpa in the Kathmandu Valley, and for inspiring a whole school of textual production and printing, sometimes referred to as “the School of Tsangnyon.” Tsangnyon practiced and disseminated the core teachings of the Kagyu tradition: the Six Dharmas of Nāropa, Mahāmudrā, and the Aural Transmissions that had been transmitted by Milarepa’s closest disciples. [rigpa-wiki:Tennyi Yungdrung Lingpa] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tennyi-lingpa] Tennyi Lingpa Pema Tsewang Gyelpo was a fifteenth-century treasure revealer whose literary work escapes the sectarian confines of Tibetan religious traditions. Although he was originally trained mainly as a Drukpa Kagyu practitioner, the center of gravity of his interests seems to have shifted towards the Nyingma tradition around his forties, after he met Pema Lingpa and became his disciple not long before the latter's death in 1521. He later played an important role in the history of the Gungtang Kingdom and is counted as a major figure in the Northern Treasures tradition because he found a terma said to have been discovered and then re-hidden by Rigdzin Godemchen , which complements a cycle of practice that is crucial to the Northern Treasures. He is counted as one of the "eight lingpas." (BDRC P1697)

Born in present day Mustang, Nepal, he traveled widely around Tibet promoting the Jangter tradition with his brother, Lekden Dorje . He is remembered to have strictly observed his monastic vows and was the author of many texts, including Ascertaining the Three Vows , which lays out the Buddhist path according to the Nyingma tradition. items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:lobzang-chokyi-gyeltsen] The Fourth Paṇchen Lama, Lobzang Chokyi Gyeltsen, who was the first to hold the title, lived during a time of tremendous political and religious change in Tibet. During his near-century long life the Geluk government of the Fifth Dalai Lama , the Ganden Podrang, took power in Tibet, and Bhutan established itself as an independent state under the rule of the Drukpa Kagyu, both events in which he was intimately connected. Lobzang Chokyi Gyeltsen was a teacher to many powerful Tibetan, Bhutanese and Mongolian political and religious figures, including the Fourth and the Fifth Dalai Lamas, and the First Jetsundampa of Mongolia. The Sixteenth abbot of Tashilhunpo , he was given the title Paṇchen Lama by the Fifth Dalai Lama, who declared him an emanation of Amitabha. [rigpa-wiki:Taktsang Lotsawa Sherab Rinchen] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:taktsang-repa-ngawang-gyatso] Taktsang Repa Ngawang Gyatso was an important Drukpa Kagyu patriarch and a key figure in the religious history of Ladakh, where he worked with the expansionist king Sengge Namgyel to make the Drukpa tradition dominant in the kingdom. He is famous for making several journeys across Central Asia, visiting Emei Shan in China, numerous sites in southern Tibet connected to Milarepa , and historically Buddhist kingdoms in Northern India. In Ladakh he founded Hanle Monastery and restored Hemis Monastery , which his incarnations have continued to lead. (BDRC P7857)

Marin Mersenne was a French philosopher, theologian, and mathematician known for his role in the scientific revolution. Although a firm advocate of Catholic orthodoxy, Mersenne corresponded with many of the leading intellectuals of his time, including Descartes, Galileo, and Gassendi. His engagement with skepticism was significant; Mersenne critiqued Pyrrhonism, emphasizing that while human knowledge has limits, faith provides a foundation for certainty. Mersenne’s skeptical but methodical approach to scientific inquiry also laid the groundwork for later Cartesian and empiricist traditions.

items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:ngawang-lobzang-gyatso] The Fifth Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobzang Gyatso, popularly known "The Great Fifth", was the first dalai lama to assume political rule of Tibet, forging lasting alliances with Mongol armies and the Qing court in China. He was both a brilliant tactician and a religious thinker, authoring numerous commentaries and ritual manuals, as well as histories and biographies. Although responsible for considerable sectarian violence and Geluk hegemony, including the suppression in Tibet of the Jonang tradition and the forcible conversion of many monasteries to the Geluk faith, the Fifth Dalai Lama never abandoned his family’s Nyingma affiliations, and he sponsored the establishment or renovation of several Nyingma monasteries. items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tendzin-rabgye] Tenzin Rabgye was a seventeenth century Bhutanese religious and political leader in whose personage the lineages of two major figures in Bhutanese history, Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyel and Drukpa Kunle , were joined. Among his many treasures included in the Rinchen Terdzod are the Namcho cycle, for which he is best known. He became posthumously known as the First Seula Tulku , beginning an important incarnation line in Bhutan. (BDRC P529)

A French philosopher, Robinet is one of the early figures to propose that evolution is driven by a spiritual force or energy. Although later ridiculed for his belief in mermaids, Robinet’s ideas about spiritual evolution helped lay the groundwork for future explorations into the relationship between spirit and matter in the natural world.

A German polymath, Goethe embraced the concept of spiritual evolution, particularly in the realm of plant morphology. His theory on the development of plants inspired both philosophers like Friedrich Schelling and naturalists like Charles Darwin. Goethe’s understanding of nature as a dynamic, evolving force deeply influenced subsequent generations of thinkers.

Thomas Taylor was an English translator and Neoplatonist, renowned for being the first to translate the complete works of Aristotle and Plato into English, as well as the Orphic fragments. His translations were instrumental in reviving interest in ancient Greek philosophy during the 18th and 19th centuries. Taylor's work was deeply influenced by the Neoplatonic tradition, and he sought to convey the metaphysical and spiritual dimensions of Platonic and Aristotelian thought to a wider audience as part of his dedication to their revival.

[rigpa-wiki:Könchok Lhundrup] [rigpa-wiki:Könchok Gyurme Tenpé Gyaltsen] [lotsawa-house:lotsawa-tibetan:konchok-tenpe-dronme] [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:konchok-gyeltsen] Konchok Gyeltsen was a Barawa lama active in Tibet, Bhutan, and Sikkim during the seventeenth century. He is counted among the "five lama factions" in Bhutan that did not support  Zhabdrung Rinpoche 's unification of the country and, as a result, he was forced to leave Bhutan, after which the Barawa monasteries were taken over by the Drukpa Kagyu. Relocating to Sikkim, he established the Barawa tradition there with the sponsorship of the first Buddhist ruler. His incarnation line is known as the Kagyu Tulkus and also the Drubtob Tulkus. (BDRC P7118)

Developed transcendental idealism, emphasizing the unity of subject and object in the pursuit of spiritual development and self-realization. A German philosopher and a student of Kant, Fichte argued that both subjective mind and objective nature are evolving expressions of a transcendent consciousness. He viewed the individual self as part of a broader, ongoing process of spiritual evolution, anticipating themes later explored in process philosophy and integral theory.

A German idealist philosopher, Hegel’s philosophy of history and dialectics sees Spirit (Geist) unfolding through historical processes, eventually achieving self-awareness. His work strongly influenced later developmental thinkers, emphasizing that reality evolves through dialectical processes, uniting opposites in a higher synthesis.

Krause is best known for his philosophy of Panentheism known as Krausism, which posits that God is both immanent within the universe and transcendent beyond it. His concept of Panentheism sought to reconcile Pantheism and Theism, asserting that everything exists in God, but God’s essence surpasses the material universe. He coined the term Panentheism to describe this framework. Krause’s work laid a foundation for evolutionary and process theology, influencing later thinkers who explored the dynamic relationship between God, nature, and human development. He also promoted a vision of universal harmony and moral progress, emphasizing that humanity’s ultimate goal is to achieve a higher consciousness aligned with divine order.

Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher best known for his work The World as Will and Representation (1818). He emphasized the role of the will—a blind, irrational force underlying all of reality—over reason and intellect, which he saw as secondary. Schopenhauer was heavily influenced by both Plato and Kant, but he also drew deeply from Eastern philosophies, particularly Hinduism and Buddhism. His concept of the will to live resonates with Eastern ideas of desire (tanha) and the suffering caused by attachment. Schopenhauer believed that asceticism, aesthetic contemplation, and compassion could offer liberation from the painful cycle of will and suffering, making him a key figure in the development of pessimistic philosophy. His work significantly influenced later existentialist and nihilist thinkers, including Nietzsche and Freud.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jamgon-kongtrul-lodro-taye] Jamgon Kongtrul is often described as one of the greatest scholars in the history of Tibet. A Karma Kagyu lama and model of rime  ecumenical activity, he collaborated closely with the Sakya lama Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and the Nyingma treasure revealer Chokgyur Lingpa , in the opening of sacred sites and the revelation of treasure. His prodigious literary output, categorized as the Five Treasuries , cover the entire range of Tibetan Buddhist theory and ritual as well as numerous other topics, and preserved scores of Tibetan religious traditions that were at the time in danger of being lost. Based primarily at Pelpung Monastery, in Derge in eastern Tibet, he built the nearby hermitage of Tsadra Rinchen Drak , which became his personal seat. Multiple incarnation lines were recognized after his death, including the main Jamgon Ko…

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jangchub-tsondru] Jangchub Tsondru was a chief lama to the important Bhutanese leader, Trongsa Ponlob Jigme Namgyel, and the inventor of the “Jarog Dongchen” headgear which protects him. Born in southern Tibet, he was associated with Bhutan at a young age and spent most of his life travelling between Tibet and Bhutan, and especially between Lhodrak and Bumtang. He was a free spirit, travelling almost incessantly, interested in teachings from different religious schools, and detached from material possessions. He also appears to have been a powerful and much sought after lama, said to be able to subdue two categories of spirits, the lu and the gyelpo . (BDRC P862)

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:jamyang-khyentse-wangpo] Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo was one of the most prominent lamas of the nineteenth century of any tradition. He is said to have received teachings from over one hundred and fifty lamas of all traditions, including, possibly, Bon, and served as teacher to most of the lamas of Kham in the second half of the nineteenth century. From his seat at Dzongsar Monastery in Derge, a branch of Ngor , he traveled twice to Tibet, and endlessly traversed Kham teaching and performing religious rituals. He famously worked closely with Jamgon Kongtrul and Chokgyur Lingpa , at the center of a religious revival the effects of which are still being felt. He was involved with the creation of Jamgon Kongtrul’s “Five Treasuries” and assisted Chokgyur Lingpa with the production of most of his treasures, authorizing and providing the organization of the revelations…

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:chokgyur-lingpa] Chokgyur Lingpa was one of the most prolific treasure revealers of the nineteenth century. Based in Kham, he was a close collaborator with Jamgon Kongtrul and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo , with whom he revealed treasure and opened sacred sites. Among his best-known revelations are the Dispelling all Obstacles, or Barche Kunsel, the Seven Profound Cycles, or Zabpa Kor Dun, and the Gradual Path of the Wisdom Essence, or Lamrim Yeshe Nyingpo, for which Jamgon Kongtrul wrote a famous commentary. Chokgyur Lingpa also revealed an enumeration of great sites in Khams that had a significant impact on the sacred geography of the region. He established two monastic centers, Tsike and Netan , seats of the Tsike and Neten lines of his reincarnation. (BDRC P564)

A Ukrainian mystic and founder of the Theosophical Society, Blavatsky was instrumental in the resurgence of esoteric thought in the late 19th century. Her writings introduced the idea of spiritual evolution, emphasizing the progression of the soul through reincarnation and the role of hidden knowledge in guiding human development.
[lineage-seed:modern-spiritual:olcott] Co-founder and first president of the Theosophical Society. Worked with Blavatsky to establish the society in New York and later Adyar, India.
[lineage-seed:modern-spiritual:ramakrishna] Root of the modern Vedanta missionary line. His direct disciples established the Ramakrishna Mission and spread Hindu contemplative teaching globally.

[lineage-seed:ramakrishna-lineage:ramakrishna] Root of this chart. Bengali mystic and priest at the Kali Temple of Dakshineswar. Core teachings: Realization of God through many paths, bhakti and jnana as complementary, and direct experience over mere doctrine. His direct monastic and householder disciples formed the Ramakrishna Order and preserved his teachings in the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna.

items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:tana-lhatse-tulku-karma-ngawang-drakpa-chokdrub] Karma Ngawang Drakpa Chokdrub, who would posthumously be known as the First Lhatse Tulku, was a nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Yelpa Kagyu lama based at Jang Tana Monastery . He was a student of the First Tsoknyi and the Dabzang Karma Ngedon Tenpa Rabgye . He should not be confused with the Lhatse Tulku line affiliated with Pelyul Monastery .

A Canadian psychiatrist, Bucke is known for his book Cosmic Consciousness, where he cataloged the evolution of human consciousness through mystical experiences. He theorized that humanity is progressing toward a future state of cosmic consciousness, where individuals attain unity with the divine and an awareness of the cosmic order.

[lineage-seed:kriya-yoga-lineage:shirdi-sai-baba] Saint of Shirdi; initiated by Lahiri Mahasaya in the Kriya line according to Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi and related devotional tradition. Forced removal of Cherokee people from the southeastern US.

items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:fifth-drubgyud-tulku-drubgyud-tulku] The Fifth Drubgyud Tulku was a nineteenth-century Yelpa Kagyu lama based at Tana Monastery. He was a student of the Fourteenth Karmapa and the Ninth Tai Situ .
Agreement between the Crown and Māori chiefs.

[rigpa-wiki:Shri Singha] [lineage-seed:nisargadatta-lineage:bhausaheb] Disciple of Nimbargi Maharaj who established the Inchegeri branch of the Navnath sampradaya. Taught mantra-meditation (Pipilika Marg, the Ant's Way) to householders including Siddharameshwar Maharaj.

[lineage-seed:inchagiri-sampradaya:bhausaheb] Disciple of Nimbargi Maharaj who established the Inchagiri sampradaya. Taught Nama-Yoga / Jnana Marga, remembered as the Pipilika Marg (Ant's Way) of mantra-meditation.
Founded by Bahá'u'lláh, emphasizes unity of all religions and humanity
[lineage-seed:ramakrishna-lineage:girish-ghosh] Leading householder disciple, playwright, and exemplar of Ramakrishna's teaching for those living in the world.
[lineage-seed:kriya-yoga-lineage:panchanan] Early direct disciple of Lahiri Mahasaya who published and preserved Lahiri's scriptural commentaries and Kriya teachings.
[lineage-seed:jonang-lineage:bamda-gelek-gyatso] Revived zhentong literature in Kham.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:bamda-gelek] Bamda Gelek, whose given name was Tubten Gelek Gyatso, was one of the greatest scholar-practitioners of the Jonang tradition. Based largely at Dzamtang , he was considered the reincarnation of various masters, including the Indian saint Candrakīrti, the siddha Nāropa, and two famous early Jonang lamas, Tāranātha and Kunga Drolchok . Because of his strong interest in the Geluk tradition, some thought him to also be an incarnation of the great Geluk scholar Jamyang Zhepa . His intellectual prowess and strong devotion to the deity Mañjuśrī, his tutelary deity, led others to surmise that he might be an emanation of the deity himself. (BDRC P4799)
Baháʼí theology describes God as the imperishable, uncreated source of all existence—personal yet unknowable directly, reflected in creation.

A German philosopher, Nietzsche introduced the concept of the Übermensch (Overman or Superman) as a symbol of humanity’s potential to evolve beyond traditional moral and cultural limitations. His focus on self-overcoming and the will to power parallels ideas of spiritual evolution and personal transformation, though through an existential lens rather than metaphysical.
Seven-storey octagonal pagoda tower built in 1844 by Emperor Thieu Tri, symbol of Hue.
[lineage-seed:new-thought:myrtle-fillmore] Co-founder of Unity and student in the Hopkins New Thought line.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:mipam-gyatso] Ju Mipam Gyatso was a prolific author who brought formal philosophical study -- including debate -- to the Nyingma tradition. Based in Kham during a period of great inter-sectarian exchange, he trained with the Kagyu lama Jamgon Kongtrul and the Sakya lama Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo , among others, even as he preserved a strong Nyingma identity. Among his works are the Beacon of Certainty and a commentary on the Ninth Chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra . In addition to his considerable literary output he spent decades of his life in retreat. (BDRC P252)

[lineage-seed:modern-spiritual:tingley] Successor to William Quan Judge as leader of the Theosophical Society in America (Point Loma line).

[lineage-seed:integral-yoga-lineage:max-theon] Polish-French occultist. Between 1905 and 1906 Mirra Alfassa studied occultism and spiritual discipline under him and his wife, Alma Théon, in Tlemcen—before she recognized Sri Aurobindo as her primary spiritual guide.
[lineage-seed:new-thought:hopkins] Teacher of New Thought who trained many founders of Unity, Divine Science, and Religious Science.
Modern and reform movements from the 19th century onward, including Navayāna, engaged Buddhism, and global lay societies.
[lineage-seed:modern-spiritual:judge] Co-founder and early vice-president of the Theosophical Society. Key organizer of the American Theosophical movement under Blavatsky.

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:pelden-chime-takpai-dorje] Pelden Chime Takpai Dorje was the forty-fifth king of Derge and one of the last to rule the kingdom. He was enthroned following the Nyarong War, and was indebted to Lhasa for Tibetan intervention. He lost the support of his local chieftains as Derge fell into factional fighting, during which his Tibetan wife and younger son attempted to supplant him. The factionalism ultimately resulted in his abduction, alongside his wife and two sons, by the Qing governor-general of Sichuan. He died in 1898 either in custody in Chengdu or soon after being released. (BDRC P00AG0401)

items.n: The Fifth Zhabdrung Sungtrul, Yeshe Ngodrub
items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:yeshe-ngodrub] Yeshe Ngodrub, the Fifth Zhabdrung Sungtrul, was an accomplished visual artist. He served as the fifty-seventh Desi, from 1903 to 1906, and the fifty-third Je Khenpo, from 1915 to 1917. He established Kunga Choling below the seat of his lineage, Paro Sang Chokhor. (BDRC P584)
[lineage-seed:modern-spiritual:sarada-devi] Holy mother of the Ramakrishna order and spiritual guide to his disciples.
[lineage-seed:ramakrishna-lineage:sarada-devi] Holy Mother of the Ramakrishna Order. Spiritual consort of Ramakrishna and guide to his disciples after his passing.

[lineage-seed:kriya-yoga-lineage:panchanan-bhattacharya] First disciple authorized by Lahiri Mahasaya to initiate others into Kriya Yoga. Born in Ahiritola, Kolkata; early brahmacharya, then householder and flower vendor after initiation in Varanasi. Founded the Arya Mission Institution (~1886), publishing Kriya texts and inexpensive Bhagavad Gita editions in Bengali and Hindi. Head of the Panchanan Bhattacharya householder lineage preserving all seven chapters of Kriya Yoga; compiled Lahiri's commentaries. Many Lahiri initiates also received advanced instruction from him. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panchanan_Bhattacharya; https://www.aryyamission.org/; https://kriyayogashram.net/kriya-yoga-lineage/; https://www.yogananda-srf.org/the-life-of-yogananda/autobiography_of_a_yogi.html

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:shakya-shri] Śākya Śrī was an influential yogic practitioner and teacher in Kham who traveled throughout the Himalaya, notably in Sikkim and Bhutan, giving teachings in Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen. A student of some of the era's greatest lamas, including the Sixth Khamtrul , Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo , and Ju Mipam Gyatso , he taught hundreds of disciples including the Tenth Drukchen and Sonam Zangpo, the brother of the first king of Bhutan. (BDRC P620)
[lineage-seed:modern-spiritual:leadbeater] Theosophical bishop and author who worked closely with Besant, shaping esoteric education and the Liberal Catholic Church line.
[lineage-seed:new-thought:charles-fillmore] Co-founder of Unity School of Christianity.

Swami Vivekananda was an Indian Hindu monk and a key figure in introducing Vedanta and Yoga to the Western world. A disciple of Ramakrishna, he was instrumental in revitalizing Hinduism in India while also fostering interfaith dialogue. His speech at the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago in 1893 brought the message of Universalism and the essential unity of all religions to a global audience. Vivekananda emphasized the spiritual and practical aspects of Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism), asserting that Brahman (the ultimate reality) is present in every individual soul (Atman). He advocated for the integration of spirituality with social action, particularly in serving the poor and uplifting the masses. His writings and speeches have profoundly influenced both Eastern and Western thought, and he is revered as a champion of religious pluralism and global spiritual unity.

He was supported the Chinese Nationalists over the Tibetan forces during the skirmish in 1917 and as a result was arrested and imprisoned in Southern Tibet. Escaping the Tibetans, Gara Lama went to China where he rose in the ranks of the government and attracted a significant number of Chinese disciples – in Chongqing he established a Buddhist center that attracted upwards of ten thousand Chinese students, becoming one of the first Tibetan lamas to translate Tibetan Buddhism for a wide Chinese audience.  Assigned by the Nationalists in the mid 1930s to help counter the Communist army in Kham, Gara Lama rebelled against the Nationalist army and declared Kham self-rule. [lineage-seed:integral-yoga-lineage:sri-aurobindo] Founder of Integral Yoga. He did not follow a traditional, long-term guru–disciple line. Independent start (1904): Began yoga on his own using guidelines from a friend who was a disciple of Brahmananda of Ganga Mutt, emphasizing pranayama and the teachings of the Gita. Lele (1908): Received crucial guidance from Vishnu Bhaskar Lele in Baroda and, within three days of intensive work, achieved the mental silence that had taken Lele seven years. Mirra Alfassa (The Mother): Met in 1914 and reunited in 1920. They established a spiritual partnership of equals in yogic realization; in 1926 he entrusted her with the Sri Aurobindo Ashram.

After reuniting in 1920 they formed a partnership of equals in yogic stature; in 1926 he entrusted her with the Ashram's direction and the development of Auroville.

A Polish-American philosopher, Korzybski founded General Semantics, exploring how language, meaning, and time shape human cognition and the evolution of consciousness, influencing later developmental models.

A revered Indian sage, Ramana Maharshi’s teachings focus on self-realization through self-inquiry. Though not professing a developmental view of consciousness and its evolution is profound enlightenment had an explosive impact on those around him. He was the fundamental catalyst of H.W.L Poonja’s awakening who was the teacher of Andrew Cohen and others.

An English Neo-Theosophist, Bailey expanded on the works of Helena Blavatsky and other occult thinkers. Her writings focused on the evolution of consciousness and the idea of a spiritual hierarchy guiding humanity’s development. Bailey’s work laid the foundation for many of the concepts found in New Age spirituality, including the belief in an esoteric and evolutionary spiritual process.

A Jesuit priest and paleontologist, Teilhard saw evolution as a process that ultimately leads to the Omega Point, where humanity and the cosmos are united in divine consciousness. Though often associated with evolutionary theology, his views align with process thought in their emphasis on dynamic becoming.

items.d: [lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:sixth-drubgyud-tulku-karma-jangchub-gyelpo] The Sixth Drubgyud Tulku, Karma Jangchub Gyelpo was a nineteenth-century Yelpa Kagyu lama based at Tana Monastery. He was a student of Fifteenth Karmapa , the Eleventh Tai Situ , and Jamyang Khyentse Chokyi Lodro .

[lineage-seed:kagyu-lineage:ngawang-tashi-dechen-dorje] Ngawang Tashi Dechen was a Ladakhi Drukpa Kagyu lama who trained and taught at Hemis , Stakna , and Bardan monasteries. He passed away young while studying in Bhutan.

[lineage-seed:kriya-yoga-lineage:motilal-mukherjee] Motilal Thakur / Mukherjee; disciple of Sri Yukteswar Giri. Sources: https://www.kararashram.org/gurus.html; https://kriyayogashram.net/kriya-yoga-lineage/

[lineage-seed:inchagiri-sampradaya:ranade] Scholar-mystic, vice-chancellor of Allahabad University, and disciple in the Amburao branch. Author and teacher of the Pipilika Marg line.

Tillich’s theology is often referred to as existentialist theology, but it also integrates ideas from Panentheism and process philosophy. His concept of God as the Ground of Being connects the divine to the evolution of consciousness and the unfolding of human history. Tillich saw God as a dynamic force active within the world, contributing to the ongoing process of human development and understanding.
[lineage-seed:new-thought:holmes] Founder of Religious Science (Science of Mind) after study with Hopkins.
